**What the London "Lancet" Says.**

LONDON, August 26th.—The Lancet says: When it is borne in mind that in cases of starvation death supervenes when the loss of two-fifths of the original weight has occurred, the fact that President Garfield has lost 80 pounds is alone sufficient to excite serious apprehension. We cannot but regard the parotid swelling or abscess as of serious import. Although it be exaggeration to speak of his recovery as altogether beyond a hope, a speedy improvement is necessary to avert the worst results.

**Vice-President Arthur.**

NEW YORK, August 26th.—Vice-President Arthur was seen at his home to-day noon. He has not been summoned, nor has he received any intimation to be in readiness to go to the capital. Should he receive such message he would go at once.

**Served Him Right.**

NEW YORK, August 26th.—Public sympathy runs decidedly with the young California lady who chastised the self-styled British Captain Burslem at West Point, for the reason that the immediate provocation for her impulsive act was only the culmination of a persistent series of unmanly and exasperating annoyances previously sustained at his hands. The lady is in great distress because of the unexpected publicity she has achieved, but the general verdict is that she served him right.

**Business Failures.**

NEW YORK, August 26th.—The failures during the week have been rather more numerous than usual, numbering 113, of which there were 24 in the Middle States, 15 in the Eastern, 21 in the Southern, 40 in the Western, and 12 on the Pacific coast. In point of liabilities the failures have been light, and when the petty retail cases have been deducted very few remain calling for attention or remark.

**A Treacherous Friend.**

NEW YORK, August 26th.—W. Penny, kid glove manufacturer here, died two years ago, recommending his wife to his friend and associate, Julius Loewey, for assistance in managing her fortune of $100,000. Julius took hold at once, and now turns up an absconder to the amount of $16,000 at least. He is somewhere in Europe. Lawyers and detectives are after him.

City Marshal Murdered by Roughs.
SILVERTON, August 26th.—Last night D. C. Osbury, City Marshal, was killed by two roughs named Burt Wilkinson and Dyson H. Bridge. The whole town is aroused, and the murderers will be lynched if captured. Bridge is a notorious desperado, and large rewards are offered for his arrest for other crimes.

Powder Mill Blown Up.
WARREN (Me.), August 26th.—The building of Watson, Burrel & Co.'s powder manufactory exploded to-day, destroying a ton of fine powder. Samuel Monk was blown 400 feet and killed. Loss, $10,000.

CONVICTED OF MURDER. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
KANSAS CITY, Mo., Sept. 5.—At 11 o'clock tonight the jury in the Charles Jefferson murder case brought in a verdict of guilty in the first degree, and the man must hang. Jefferson killed a man last fall in a tenement-house on Fifth street in this city, but claimed it was in self-defense. His wife or mistress witnessed the killing, and at the preliminary examination swore to the fact. About two months ago the woman died suddenly from poison, but her testimony before the justice was admitted as evidence, and mainly by it the man was found guilty.

ARREST OF MURDERERS.

ARREST OF MURDERERS.
DENVER, Col., Sept. 5.—Ten days ago D. C. Ogsbury, City Marshal of Silverton, was murdered by Bert Wilkinson, a well-known deserado, while attempting to quell a disturbance in which Wilkinson and two companions, the one named Eskridge and the other a negro boy, had become involved. The negro surrendered to the authorities, and the Vigilance Committee of Silverton hung him the night after Ogsbury's murder. Wilkinson and Eskridge betook themselves to the neighborhood of the Needle Mountain, which lies close to Durango, where they have just been captured.

CHARGED WITH THEFT.
Bpecial Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

WINONA, Minn., Sept. 5.—William Gunn, bookkeeper of the L. C. Porter Milling Company, was arrested Saturday night on a charge of embezzlement. Gunn's duty was to pay for what wheat was purchased, consequently large sums passed through his hands. The stealings have been systematically going on for the past year, and foots up $800 or $1,000. Gunn has moved in the best society, but has been fast and lived beyond his means. He was suspected some time ago of irregularities, and a detective was employed to shadow him.

WAYLAID AND KILLED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LITTLE Rock, Ark., Sept. 5.—Advices from War Eagle, Carroll County, say that Jasper Evans, a prominent citizen, was waylaid and killed while feeding his horses just at nightfall on Sunday. The wife of the slain man ran to the door upon hearing the discharge of a gun, and, hurrying out, found her husband dead, with two bullets in his back. She saw two men disappearing in the edge of an adjacent wood. The murderers have since been captured and jailed. The affair grew out of an old feud.

RETIREMENT OF SURGEONS. Woodward: Reyburn and Barnes Retire from President's Case.
At a late hour to-night the agent of the National Associated Press received definite information that the rumors about the retirement of three of the physicians from the president's case were about to be confirmed. The information came direct from those most interested, and cannot be mistaken. Drs. Barnes, Woodward and Reyburn signed the bulletin to-night for the last time, and to-morrow the early bulletin will contain the official announcement of the fact that hereafter Dr. Bliss will have full control of the case with Drs. Agnew and Hamilton consulting physicians. One of them is to be with Dr. Bliss all the time. Intimations of such an occurrence have been given from time to time, but it was not until to-night that the fact was in any way established. Dr. Bliss stated that the change was made in deference to the wish of the president and not on account of any difference between the physicians in the case. He did not think the president had any particular reason for dsiring such a change beyond a wish to have fewer attendants and more quiet. "Sickmen's wishes," said Dr. Bliss, "are not always easily explained."

Further inquiry to-night shows the facts to be about as follows: On Saturday last the event of the project of the journey was being definitely considered. The president said to Mrs. Garfield: "What is the use of all the physicians going to Long Branch?" The remark so impressed Mrs. Garfield that she mentioned it to one of the physicians, and they talked it over together. Meanwhile the president had said that he thought Dr. Bliss will be enough to take care of him, with Dr Agnew and Dr. Hamilton. to consult with him. Under the circumstances it was particularly referred to Dr. Agnew for his advice. He, in turn, thought that the physicians the president proposed to eliminate ought to be the ones to speak. Dr. Woodward, it seems, was anxious to retire and both Drs. Reyburn and Surgeon General Barnes had business in Washington which they could ill afford to neglect. So the arrangement above referred to was made.

OFFICIAL BULLETIN.

LONG BRANCH, Sept. 7.—Elberon 9 a. m.—The president slept the greater of the night, awakening, however, as often as it was necessary to give him nourishment, which he took very well. The fever reported in last evening's bulletin had subsided by 11 p. m. This morning his temperature is not normal and he appears to have recovered from the fatigue of yesterday's journey. At the morning dressing the parotid abscess was found to be doing well. The visible parts of the wound look somewhat better. Pulse 106, temperature 98.4, respiration 18. The next bulletin will be issued at 8 p. m.

(Signed) D. H. AGNEW,
D. W. BLISS,
J. J. WOODWARD,
R. REYBURN,

OFFICIAL BULLETIN.

ELBERON, September 7, 6 p. m.— Notwithstanding the exceptional heat of the weather, the thermometer is only 94 in the president's bedroom at 3:30 this afternoon. There was a breeze most of the day, so that the president was comparatively comfortable. He has taken his nourishment regularly and slept at regular intervals during the day. At 12:15 p. m. his pulse was 114, temperature 98.4 and respiration 18. Since then there has been some rise of temperature,

though less than yesterday, and the pulse has somewhat diminished in frequency. At the evening dressing the appearance of the wound was favorable. At present his pulse is 108, temperature 101, respiration 18.
(Signed) F. H. HAMILTON.
D. W. BLISS,
J. W. BARNES,
J. J. WOODWARD,
ELEVEN P. M. BULLETN.

The president's fever has subsided and he has thus far passed as good a night as last night.

BEATEN.

The Republicans of San Francisco Suffer an Unexpected Defeat.

Special Dispatch to THE BEE.

SAN FRANCISCO, September 7.—The election to-day is supposed to be in favor of the democracy by 3,000, which elects the whole ticket, from mayor down to school director. Possibly two or three republican supervisors may run ahead enough to be elected, but at present it looks like a clean sweep. The causes for a republican defeat are said to be that the milkmen, a new element in politics, put up the convention to shut out Higgins and Chute and then Higgins and Chute shut out the ticket by declining to vote for the nominees.

NEW JERSEY'S HEATED TERM.

Cattle and Crops Suffering and Things Generally Dried Up.

National Associated Press.

LONG BRANCH, September 7. — The entire New Jersey southern coast is suffering indescribably from terrible heat and prolonged drouth. All the streams and ponds in Ocean and Monmouth counties are dried up and the spring are giving out. Cattle are dying for want of water, and where water can be obtained the pastures are parched and dried up. Wood fires in Alsion, Shamony and Whitings are spreading with alarming rapidity and only copious showers will stop the work of destruction.

The heat at the Branch is oppressive, the thermometer reaching as high as 104° in the shade. Directly on the beach at Barnegat the thermometer at noon was 105° in the shade. At Freehold the thermometer was as high as 106° in the shade; also at South Amboy 107°, at Red Bank 104°. The ocean is as calm as a mill pond and the little breezes that come from the west feel like gusts from a fireroom.

Summary Disposal of Three Men Interested in Oglesby's Murder.

Oglesby, city marshal of Silverton, was murdered by Bert Wilkinson, a desperado, while trying to quell a disturbance in which Wilkinson and two companions, Eskridge and a negro boy, had become involved. The negro surrendered and the vigilance committee of Silverton hung him. Wilkinson and Eskridge have just been captured and it is rumored that they were hanged by the mob last night.

CINCINNATI'S GALA WEEK.

The Exposition, Soldiers' Reunion and Other Celebrations.

CINCINNATI, O., September 7.—The city is gaily arrayed in evergreens and hunting, and the streets are thronged with strangers from all parts of the country. The exposition throws open its doors at noon. The present month promises to be one of the most busy in the history of the city. Besides the esposition and massive conclave, there is to be a soldiers' reunion, which is expected to be the largest since the war, Odd Fellows' reunion, and some dozen other unimportant state and national gatherings.

BRADFORD, Pa., September 7.—Heavy forest fires raged this afternoon near Coleville, the eastern portion of the oil district, two miles from this place. Thirty to forty oil rigs, with tanks and oil, were consumed, causing an aggregate loss of many thousand dollars. LYNCHED.
Special Correspondence of The Chicago Tribune,
Rico, Colo., Sept. 10. About 9:30 last Sunday evening the closing scene of a most thrilling tragedy was played at Silverton, thirty-five miles northeast of here. Some days before a promiscuous shooting-match had occurred in a saloon several miles north of Durango, on the Durango and Silverton toll-road. During the molle the salookeeper was killed, but no one know who fired the fatal shot. Hert Wilkinson and a "coon" named Jim Catrin, both of whom had figured prominently in the row, immediately made themselves scarce, and shortly afterwards turned up, in company with Dison Eskridge, on the streets of Silverton. Eskridge, who had been here for some time attending to mining interests, had started for Durango the morning of the day on which the shooting occurred. It is claimed that he was not present when the saloonkeeper was killed. The Marshal of Silverton, Clate Ogsbury, attempted to arrest the party, and was

KILLED ALMOST INSTANTLY, living only long enough to state that Wilkinson was the one to whom he owed his death.

The three at once fled, but nearly 100 men were upon their track within a few minutes. Catrin was caught the next day and lodged in the Silverton Jail, from which he was taken the same evening and lynch law most effectively dealt out to him. A reward of $5,500 was offered for the delivery, dead or alive, to the Sheriff of San Juan County, of Wilkinson and Eskridge. The latter is still at liberty. The former was captured by the notorious Ike Stockton, for whom Wilkinson would have risked his life at any time, of which fact Stockton was perfectly aware. The following account of the capture was given by Mrs. Flora W. Pyle, the sister of Wilkinson, who resides at Castle Rock Springs. The statement of Mrs. Pyle was taken verbatim by a special reporter of the Dolores News, and is the only true and accurate account yet given:

"My brother (A. W. Wilkinson) and Dison Eskridge came to our house at 12 o'clock at night on Sunday. They knocked at the door gently, and I answered the call, asking who was there. The answer was, 'Bert.' When I recognized Bert his first words were: 'Flora, we are awful hungry, but have you got anything that will fit Dison's feet; he is barefooted. He then asked if I had anything cooked. I gave them a lunch, which they ate outdoors. They did not enter the house during the time they were hereabouts.

IKE STOCKTON

had arrived here in the evening preceding that night, and was then sleeping in the house across the way. I told the boys of this, when they seemed to be overjoyed, and expressed a desire to see him immediately. Stockton was then sent for, and when he came over to see them he remarked: It is very cold this evening! His teeth were chattering, he was trembling, and I suppose he made this remark to hide the true cause of his nervousness, which was that his conscience smote him for the treachery he was practicing toward his friend, whom he intended to deliver up to be hanged for money's sake. Stockton had been to my house for supper, and returned for breakfast, at the request of a friend, Mr. Welfoot, who had the hospitality of our home. I had made every arrangement for the boys to get horses and provisions with which to continue their travels. I aided in their escape (so far as they went), and if it be criminal I would not regret it, for Bert was my brother, and Dlson his sworn friend. Had I not done as I did, I would feel that I were inhuman. Bert asked who was blamed for the shooting, but did not deny or acknowledge that he killed the Marshal, as he could not know. Mr. Stockton said when he came to our house that night that he had heard that a party would arrive from Silverton, and that he

HAD COME TO WARN THE BOYS, if here. After the boys had eaten their lunch, I was conversing with them at the door. Dlson said to tell his brother Arg that he and Bert would go to their brother, Dow Eskridge, and from his place on to the plains. I am told by witnesses to their arrangement that Stockton tried to have the boys separate, saying that they could escape much easier in that way. They had horses, and provisions to lust them four or five days. They both said while here that when they had reached a place where they could go to work and behave themselves they would do so, and in the future live and act honorably.

"Stockton, when asked in to breakfast, said he was not hungry, but sat down to the table and ate a hearty breakfast, conversing freely all the while about matters of small consequence, and wanted Mr. Welfoot to go to Farmington with him. He had a great deal to say about his living in dread of the law, and said many of his friends had advised him to leave this country and change his name, etc. The manner in which STOCKTON, AS A COMBADE, CAPTURED BERT has caused him to say much to vindicate his treacherous action. He seems to think he has a statement to make to all he meets, separately and collectively. He says that Bert owed him $19 and refused to pay it.

"Bert told me after his capture that he and Dlson went to the place agreed on with Stockton the night they were here, and Stockton and Cook came to them in the morning. Stockton said he would have to go to the Florida after fresh horses. He left Bert and Cook and took Dlson with him. He was gone till 3 o'clock in the afternoon and returned without Dlson. He told Bert that Dlson and Arg were to meet them five miles below with fresh horses. Bert got up and left his pistol on a blanket on which he had been lying. The horse was five or six yards from him, and as he started for him Stockton jumped in between him and his pistol and told him to throw up his hands. Bert did so, laughing, thinking it was a joke; but seeing Stockton's face the truth commenced to dawn on him, and he said: 'Ike, do you mean it?' to which Stockton replied: 'Yes, I do mean it. Money is what makes men in this country. Bert said: 'You've got the drop on me. Ike, but I'd rather you'd kill me.' Stockton promised him he'd never be turned over without something to defend himself with."

AFTER HIS CAPTURE

he was kept under a strong guard at Animal City until Saturday, when he was turned over to the Sheriff of San Juan County, who took him to Silverton and lodged him in jail. He was accompanied by his sister, who remained in Silverton till Sunday. It was no doubt, due to her presence that he was no lynched Saturday night. She was informed Sunday that he would be hanged whether she remained in town or not, and that if she went her brother's body would be sent to her. Between 9 and 10 o'clock Sunday evening a party of masked men broke into the jail, took Wilkinson out, and made summaries preparations for launching him into the green beyond. Up to the last moment he showed the utmost fortitude, and died "the gamer of the game." As the preparations neared completion, he took the rope in his hands and with the remark

"BOYS, I'LL HELP YOU ALL I CAN," adjusted the noose about his own neck, and after expressing his regrets that he could shoot Stockton before going, "who," he said, "sold me for my blood-money," and requesting that his body should not be photographed, kicked the chair upon his stoop from under, and paid in full the debt crime which he had incurred.

LATEST NEWS
—A London dispatch states that France and England have agreed on an Anglo-French military commission for the reorganization of the Egyptian army so as to prevent future annoyance to either nation.

—John W. Brooks, of Boston, the famous railroad manager, died at Heidelberg, Germany, in his 63d year. He constructed the Boston and Maine road, negotiated the purchase of the Michigan Central by Boston capitalists, built various sections of the Burlington road, and was Chairman of the Hoosac tunnel commission.

—Dr. Lugenbeel, a brother of Mrs. Christiancy, sent a formal challenge to the ex-Minister, which was declined, and a warrant asked for. The cause was reflections upon her testimony in the divorce suit.

—Portions of Iowa, Minnesota, Michigan and Nebraska, were visited by a slight snow-fall on the 16th of September.

—The New York Prohibitionists have nominated a full ticket for State officers, to be voted for at the November election.

—The value of buildings erected in Chicago, so far this year, approximates $10,275,000.

—Wheat along the Canadian Pacific road in Manitoba is said to average fully twenty-five bushels per acre, oats sixty and barley thirty.

—The Department of Agriculture reports the general average of the potato crop in the seven chief States at 68.

—Dr. Hutchinson, of Fulton county, Ark., went down into a well on his premises for the purpose of cleaning it out, and was overcome by foul air. A neighbor, while in the act of descending to his assistance, fell to the bottom of the well and broke his neck. A second neighbor descended the deadly pit and he, too, was overcome by and died from the effects of the foul gases. A number of persons, attracted by the frantic cries of Mrs. Hutchinson, gathered at the spot, and the bodies of the three dead men were taken from the well. To cap the climax of the horror, Mrs. Hutchinson has gone crazy with grief.

- Nearly $150,000 worth of property has been swept away by fire at East Rome, N. Y.

- A west-bound train from Vicksburg, Miss., ran off the track near Edwards' Depot. A sleeping-car, a passenger car and a Superintendent's car were wrecked. Many passengers were injured, six rather seriously.

- Bert Wilkinson, who during the past year killed no less than three men, was lynched at Silverton, Col.

- A negro woman was roasted alive at Dyke's Mills, La., by a mob of citizens, for having murdered two little children.

- The residence of Mrs. Jane Shiers, near Gastonia, N. C., was blown up by dynamite while she was absent. Charles Deplace, a discarded paramour, is believed to have perpetrated the deed, in the hope of extinguishing a rival.

WHOLESALE SHOOTING IN BALTIMORE YESTERDAY.—There were eight or ten persons seriously wounded by pistol-shots in Baltimore yesterday, several of whom it is feared will die. Wm. Hecker, living on Peach alley, was shot through the chest, as is alleged, by Thos. H. Ross, colored. Wm. Cuddy is under arrest, charged with shooting Carrie Sonnenburg, a young daughter of Mr. C. K. Sonnenburg, living corner of Baltimore and Arch streets. Sydney Solomon, aged 14, living on the southeast corner of Baltimore and Amity streets, was accidently shot in the back by a boy named Michael Dorn. Isaac Curtis, colored, was shot in the ablomen and fatally wounded by some one unknown.

Shooting Cases in Baltimore.
BALTIMORE, July 4.—Several cases of shooting have occurred in this city to-day. A difficulty occurred in South Baltimore between whites and blacks, in which William Hecker, a white man who was near, was shot, and his life is despaired of. Thomas H. Ross, colored, was arrested on the charge of shooting him. Isaac Curtis, colored, who was engaged in the affray was shot, and his wound is thought to be mortal. In the northern section of the city Miss Mary F. Geblin was looking from a second-story window, when John Carr, aged 17, fired upward and the ball from his pistol entered one of her eyes and killed her. Several other persons were shot, but as far as can be learned none seriously.

BALTIMORE'S Fourth of July—The City Keeps up its Reputation. BALTIMORE, July 4.—There were several shooting casualties to-day. Mary A. Givelin, while looking out of a window, was shot dead by a youth carelessly firing a pistol in the air. During a fight in South Baltimore, between the whites and blacks, William Heener, white, and Isaac Curtis, colored, were fatally wounded. Crowds of people gathered around the bulletin-boards, anxious to learn the condition of President Garfield. In all the Catholic churches special masses were offered that he may be spared to the country. The City Council is called to meet to-morrow to express the sense of the city on the terrible outrage which has been perpetrated. The display of fireworks is postponed. A FRENCH OPINION Of the American Constitution Not Without Interest.
PARIS, July 4.—Le Temps in discussing the ultimate consequences to the United States, should President Garfield die, remarked: "How greatly the rigidity of American constitutional institutions, which are based on the absolute principle of separating the powers of the legislature from those of the executive, and on the mutual independence of the President and Congress, multiplies the chances of conflict, which can only be solved after the expiration of a fixed term; whereas, the English parliamentary system of responsible government settles the difficulties by an appeal to the people, or by a modification of the ministry."

GLADSTONE

On the Attempt upon the Life of President Garfield.

LONDON, July 4.—Mr. Gladstone's statement in the House of Commons to-day, respecting the attempt on President Garfield's life, was as follows: "We cannot be surprised that the question has arisen in regard to the inspiration of the outrage upon President Garfield, the character of which is such as to attract the attention of the whole civilized world, and which so greatly affects the feelings and welfare of a nation which is not only friendly to us, but which is growing more friendly yearly. The public has been supplied with extraordinary rapidity with information of all the fluctuations in the terrible trial which the President has been called upon to undergo."

In the House of Lords Earl Granville said the sympathy of all classes in England was increased every hour, and that it was not less strong than that felt in America itself.

SEVEN PERSONS KILLED

And a Dozen Wounded Through a Forgetful Engineer.

CINCINNATI, July 4.—Seven persons were killed and twelve others wounded by an accident on the Kentucky Central railroad, twelve miles south of Covington, this afternoon about three o'clock. All were residents of Covington. The names of the killed are: John Rye, Michael Dixon, William Callopy William Wiechouf, John Caller, and two boys, names unknown, who were stealing a ride. John Rye was a fireman, the others were passengers. The wounded are: George Callopy, both legs broken and otherwise bruised; John Carney, nose and face badly bruised; Mrs. Brown, leg broken; Paul Sheridan bruised badly; John McDonald, left leg and collar-bone broken; John Rush, leg broken; John Cochran, left arm broken and scalded; Maggie Carey, scalded badly; James Crow, bruised internally; John Bethel, bruised leg and knee; Ed Hayne, cheek cut. It was a collision of the south-bound Lexington express with a picnic excursion, which was backing north for another load. The train-dispatcher ordered Conductor Frank Matlock to side-track at Culbertson Station and let the picnic train pass. The conductor gave the orders to Jake Matlock, engineer, who forget them, and passed the station. The collision was in a deep curved cut. Both the locomotives are a total wreck.

GRAIN IN EUROPE.

Weekly Review of the Foreign Breadstuffs Markets.

LONDON, July 4.—The Mark Lane Express in its review of the grain trade for the past week, says the weather has been uninterruptedly fine and wheat has passed through the critical blossoming period favorably. In regard to barley, appearances indicate a good crop on the best land and variable elsewhere. The oats prospect is bad, and appears to be the worst. Regarding trade, on account of scarcity, native wheats advanced both in London and the

provinces, and the advance was maintained, but at the close buyers operated less freely. Foreign trade has been of the wane the whole week. Wheat, on Friday, was cheaper all round. The advance which was screwed out Monday was due to the small supply. This advance was lost, particularly regarding American red winter on spot. The decline amounted to 6d@1s, yet buyers hesitated. The amount on passage increased the week's supply, chiefly Indian, Russian and American. Flour maintains Monday's advance, but the demand, which has been only consumptive, is slackening. The foreign supply, chiefly Australian and European, is very large. Prices were lower it London and the provinces on Friday. Barkey was dull and rates lower where business was transacted. Oats, native and foreign, firm and dearer. Maize quiet in tone and in buyers' favor. Sales of English wheat the past week, 19,371 quarters, against 17,974 the corresponding week last year.

TUPELO, MISS.

Proceedings of the Lee County Democratic Convention.

Special to the Appeal.]

TUPELO, Miss., July 4.—The Lee county Democratic Convention met here to-day. They indorsed Senator Lamar unanimously, recommended him as his own successor, and unanimously instructed for J. M. Stone for Governor, and for J. A. Kincanon for Auditor. They expressed profound regret at the attempted assassination of the President, and sympathy for him, and an earnest hope for his speedy recovery.

JACKSON, TENN.

Meeting of Citizens—Resolutions of Sorrow and Sympathy.

Special to the Appeal.]

JACKSON, July 4.—The news of the attempt to assassinate President Garfield created a profound sensation among all classes of people here. A large meeting of citizens of the city and county assembled at the Courthouse this evening and passed resolutions expressing sorrow and sympathy for President Garfield and family.

Notes and Comments.
Three horse thieves were lynched by masked men, at Springfield, Mo., last Friday night. — A part of the railroad train carrying Coup's circus was thrown from the track near Bellevue, Iowa, on Friday last by a bull who had decided to give the engine a little round just for amusement. He was amused. — A fire, supposed to have been started by a fire-cracker, destroyed forty wooden buildings in State Line, Penna., on Monday. — A fight between whites and blacks occurred in Baltimore on the Fourth. William Hecker, white, and Isaac Curtis, black, were shot, and, it is thought, fatally wounded. — City Marshal D. W. Patton and Deputy Sheriff John Mound were murdered in Fayetteville, Arkansas, by unknown assassins, on Sunday. Sheriff Daniels, of Columbia county, Arkansas, was murdered by several drunken negroes the same night. They called him out of his house and shot him down. — H. P. McGrath, the well-known owner of race horses, died on Tuesday morning at Long Branch. — The twenty-second annual festival of the North American Saengerbund, in Chicago, closed on Sunday with a mammoth picnic in a grove near that city. It is estimated that the gate receipts of the picnic were $10,000. — While Miss Mary A. Gebelin was looking from a second-story window, in Baltimore, on Monday, John Carr, a youth of seventeen, fired a pistol upward and the ball entered one of her eyes and killed her. — Griscom, the Chicago faster, walked five miles on Tuesday. — The schooner Capacity, of Wilmington, Delaware, with a cargo of coal for Galveston, went ashore on Frying Pan Shoals last Sunday afternoon, and is a total wreck. Her crew were saved. — During the firing of a salute in Lincoln, Nebraska, on the Fourth, a cannon burst, killing one man and wounding several others. One account says three men and a boy were killed. — In Philadelphia, on the Fourth, there were forty-seven arrests for violation of the fireworks laws. Only one case of injury by the use of fire arms was reported at the Pennsylvania hospital.

tom-wilson-wadesboro-1881-08.A1:
ELECTION ECHOES.
There was an ugly sequel to Oliver Dockery's speech at Wadesboro. A negro named Tom Wilson was arrested by Policemen Bruner and Brower for an indecency on the street, and violation of town laws. He resisted and snapped a pistol once or twice at the officers. They knocked him senseless with their clubs. A mob of negroes rushed upon them, with cries for blood and murder. The policemen fled into their dwellings, but would have been dragged out, and killed, had not Sheriff T. J. Hardison bravely faced the mob and held them in check till Marshal Tomlinson with an armed posse came to the rescue. Judge R. Tyler Bennett, also, appeared on horseback and commanded the peace. By his efforts the two policemen were brought to the court house and lodged in jail for the night to allow the drunken negroes to disperse and cool off. If the ringleaders be not arrested, and set to breaking rock on the Western N. C. R. R., the town of Wadesboro should repeal all law, and dismiss her police. The negro, Wilson, was not badly hurt, and walked home several miles in the country after the affray. So says the Times.

The colored vote, under the manipulation of the chairman of the Republican Executive Committee went pretty solidly against prohibition, while there was a large falling off in the white vote. To the almost solid colored vote may be attributed the defeat of the measure. It is useless now to discuss the causes of defeat. It is a defeat, and emphatic enough for all practical purposes. Those who sustained the measure have the satisfaction of knowing that the State is no worse off than she was before, and that if she is no better off it was not their fault.
